grounded_facts: Maya visually confirms the identity of the body in the bag, leading to official confirmation by Admiral McRaven.

memories.memory_text: I told Ammar he belongs to me, and the second he looked down, the guards were on him—kicking, punching—while I made sure he knew the rules: look at me, stay on the mat, don't lie, or I hurt you.
I handed Maya the ski mask at the door, telling her she might want to put it on—she looked out of place in her suit, fresh off the plane, but that intensity in her eyes made me pause.
She didn't flinch, just stared at me and asked if he was ever getting out—I said 'Never,' and meant it, feeling the weight of her gaze like she was already part of the machine.
I leaned in close, called him a disgrace to humanity, reminded him about the Western Union transfer and the 150 kilos of explosives—saw the flicker in his eyes when I roared in his face.
I laughed it off, switched tone—suddenly calm—and offered him a blanket if he'd just give up Hazem al-Kashmiri's email, watching to see if he'd bite on the deal after the noise.
I told Bradley the suspect's being a dick and that I’d need to turn up the heat to get the Saudi group—standing there, I could see Maya waiting in the holding area, quiet, like she always is.
I knocked on the glass to call Maya in, then told Bradley, 'Was I lying or what?'—her walking through that door proved I’d been right about her getting clearance.
I walked in late with Maya and told the room not to ask her about Ammar’s interrogation because she wouldn’t tell them anyway—then I nodded when Jessica asked if he was withholding.
I offered him falafel and orange juice, speaking calm like we were on the same side—letting him eat, trying to pull a name out after he admitted knowing Richard Reid.
When he started pleading and saying he didn't know, I stood up fast—pushed for a name one more time, made it clear lying means pain, just like I told him before.
I said it was on me—Ammar was my responsibility, and I meant it. When Jessica tried to absolve me, I snapped that it wasn't Zied's call, it was mine, and Maya's too.
When Maya suggested bluffing Ammar, I seized on it—London was still in play, and we had leverage. The next attack wasn't stopped, but we could still control the narrative.

I offered Ammar food and a cigarette, and when he finally looked me in the eye and started talking, I knew I had him — he gave up Hamza Rabia, Khabab al-Masri, and then the name we’d been chasing: Abu Ahmed al-Kuwaiti, bin Laden’s courier.

I sat on the couch in the back, slouched, when Bradley turned and snapped at me after I said, 'We don't know what we don't know.' I called it a tautology—flat, no emotion—and let it hang, even if he didn't like it.
I was eating my ice cream in peace, tossing little bits to the monkeys just to pass the time, and then one of them shot its hand through the bars and snatched the whole damn cone from me.
Right after the monkey took my ice cream, the guard came up and said the detainee was ready—just like that, back to work, no time to even finish a goddamn cone.
I watched from the tower as Faraj stepped into the open, saw the fear in his eyes when he realized it was a trap, and then the burkhas moved in—he never had a chance.
I asked the hooded man what music he liked—Bob Marley, reggae, Egyptian—offering to make a call, just to show I controlled even the small things.

I told him straight—'I'm bad news. I'm gonna break you.' Then I let him know I've done it before, watching him slump there, barely awake. After that, I leaned in with a question about food, like I gave a damn.
I told Maya I'm getting outta here—I've seen too many guys naked, over a hundred at this point. I need to do something normal for a while.
I warned Maya about the changing politics—she needs to be careful with detainees, and watch her back in Pakistan. Oversight is coming.

I remember the jolt in my chest when Maya's voice crackled over the speaker—'Dan, Debbie found Abu Ahmed!'—and I had to bite back the instinct to shut it down, because if there's even a thread of truth here, it changes everything.
I called her out—'In other words, you want it to be true'—because she was letting hope shape the intelligence, and that’s a liability.
After she slammed the table, I told her to calm down and then demanded she state her request—control had to be reestablished before any action.

I quoted the Quran to Wolf—'Allah rewards those who strive and fight over those that sit behind a desk'—watching him press his forehead to the prayer mat, knowing he couldn't easily dismiss a man invoking faith in his own moment of devotion.

I told him 'I ran it. I'll defend it,' offering to take full responsibility for the detainee program, knowing they'd need a body if things went south—and I was volunteering mine to get the funding approved.
I offered him a V Lamborghini—just like that—because 'friends' don't help unless the price is right, and I knew exactly how much this one cost.
I greeted the salesman with a 'As-salamu alaykum. Thanks my friend,' keeping it friendly on the surface, but I knew he was just a pawn we pulled out of bed to play our game.

I handed him the slip of paper and told him it was the terrorist’s mother—just needed her phone number. He hesitated, worried about Kuwait, but I made it clear the price would be paid somewhere else, not there.
I was in the back of the briefing room when the Director asked how close the compound was to the military academy. Maya gave the exact distance and said she was the one who found the place.
I stood in the hangar at Area 51 as the doors opened to reveal the stealth Black Hawks. The General said they hadn’t been tested with people yet. The SEALs asked questions during the briefing.

I said sixty percent, a soft sixty, because that's all the evidence supports — detainee reports are shaky, and I know how those rooms work. I could feel Maya's eyes on me after I spoke, like I'd betrayed something, but I called it like I saw it.

memories.memory_text: I read the cable about the farmer's sighting near Tora Bora—a tall man at the center of a diamond-shaped pattern with four guards—and stood by it, even when Maya dismissed it as pre-9/11 behavior.
I told them Ammar knows about the attack — we can't afford to dwell on blame, not with London still at risk.
I walked into the embassy kitchen late, poured coffee, and asked Maya how the search was going—then reminded her that facilitators come and go, but everyone wants money, one way or another.

When Maya smiled and said Al Qaeda members are radicals, not money-driven, I gave her a bigger smile and shot back that she was assuming greed wouldn't override ideology in the weaker ones—felt good to land that point.
I sat on the arm of the couch, legs crossed, staying quiet while Maya pressed Bradley about Abu Ahmed’s connection to bin Laden—I could feel Bradley notice me, but I didn’t shift or speak.

I told Maya it was time to let go of Abu Ahmed—that her obsession was putting other threats at risk—but she insisted Faraj’s lie about him was proof he mattered as much as bin Laden. I couldn’t tell if she was onto something or just seeing what she wanted to see.

One second we were talking, the next—explosion, glass shattering, bodies thrown—then Maya was pulling me up through smoke and chaos. I don’t remember the sound ending, just her grip on my arm and stumbling forward.
I hurried through the cubicles, nearly running, because the intel about the Jordanian mole was urgent and I needed to get to Maya right away.

I remember the look on Maya's face when I told her the Jords had a mole—her disbelief right before I played the video. I popped the CD in, and when Balawi appeared, I pointed him out: a Jordanian doctor, motivated, real.

I saw Maya bolt up from her chair when she realized what we had. As we walked toward Bradley's office together, I said it clearly—'This is it'—because I knew, in that moment, we had something actionable.

I told Bradley that the Jordanians had worked Balawi for a year with dinners and money, convincing him to turn on Al Qaeda for patriotism and profit—he was right there in the inner circle, and we couldn’t dismiss that without talking to him first.

I told the team Balawi wouldn't come to Islamabad—he insisted we meet him in Miram Shah or the tribal areas, and I knew that was a non-starter given the risk. When David suggested alternatives, I confirmed we weren't going to him, and after a pause, I said it plainly: we were stuck.

I was decorating a birthday cake and on the satellite phone with Washington, feeling good about the gesture, when Maya called out that Muslims don’t celebrate with cake—I paused, but stood by it, saying everyone likes cake and invited her to join anyway.
I called out to Maya from outside the Predator bay, trying to pull her away from the monitors—told her we had lots of wine, and she just stayed focused, watching the target vanish in the feed.
I poured two glasses of wine and raised a toast, saying this informant was the first big break we'd had since 9/11.

I laid out the plan—how the money could get us bin Laden in six to twelve months if the doctor didn't slip up, and if he failed, we’d eliminate him. I could see John questioning it, but the logic held.

I set the speaking order for the briefing—John would handle asset protection after I opened, then Lauren could ask her questions once Balawi had time to settle in after the basics and the birthday cake.
I reminded Lauren to give real-time updates to Washington—she confirmed she was on it, and I emphasized being concise because the Director was in the loop, possibly even updating the President.
I told the security guard to remove the gate personnel because their presence could spook my source—I insisted it was different this time, even though I couldn’t explain why.
I ran back to the team and gave a thumbs up to confirm he was on site—no hesitation, we were moving to the next phase.
I pulled out my phone, smiled, and sent the text—'He's here. Brb'—short and clear, just like comms should be under pressure.
I saw the sedan approaching, 50 yards out, and slipped the phone back into my pocket as the guard confirmed Balawi was inside.
I saw Balawi step out of the car, his hand in his pocket, and something in his movement made my smile fade just before the world exploded.

I walked into the secure CIA section of the embassy, and when Bradley asked how I liked Pakistan, I told him it was kinda fucked up — then confirmed I hadn’t volunteered for this posting.
I told Daniel and Jessica that Ammar was in the dark—we could use that. He hadn't slept, he had no idea our warning failed, and that meant we could feed him a story he'd believe.

I remember the moment in the interrogation video when the prisoner said, 'Yes, I remember him. A nice guy,' about Abu Ahmed—something in the tone made me pause and cross-reference it with nine other files open on my screen.
I watched the prisoner stare at the photograph and say 'Abu Ahmed' over and over, his voice flat but certain, while the interrogator held the image close to his face.
I was in the embassy kitchen late at night, eating something quick, when Jessica came in and made a comment about everyone wanting money—like that would apply to Al Qaeda.

I watched the prisoner study the photograph and say he recognized Abu Ahmed, then confirm he worked closely with Abu Faraj—my pulse tightened when Hakim translated that he carried messages between Faraj and bin Laden.
I leaned in and told Hakim we needed to test the prisoner’s truthfulness, and when he replied with the names of Faraj’s children, I felt the weight shift—this wasn’t just rumor, it was confirmation.

I pressed Ghul on Abu Ahmed, and when he said he was bin Laden's most trusted courier—someone who brought messages directly from the Sheikh—I felt a surge of certainty, though I tried to keep my face still.

I agreed to process a full folder of intelligence work—family ties, financial networks, all of it—just to get a one-on-one with Faraj. I didn’t need to open the folder; I already knew what it would take.
I asked Faraj what Al Buluchi looked like, and he said tall, thin, with a long white beard and a cane—details that finally gave us a physical profile after months of chasing shadows.
I found Daniel by the empty monkey cage at pre-dawn, and when he asked me to leave with him, I told him I couldn't—I wouldn't find Abu Ahmed from D.C.
I realized Faraj lying about Abu Ahmed was just like him lying about bin Laden’s location — he’s protecting someone he thinks is that important. That’s when I knew my lead was solid.
One second we were talking, the next — a deafening blast, glass flying, everything torn apart. I got up, grabbed Jessica, and pulled her out while smoke filled the room.
I saw Jessica coming toward me fast, moving through the cubicles like something urgent had just broken—her pace told me this was different.
Jessica burst in saying the Jordanians have a mole, and then played a video—I saw Balawi on screen and couldn't believe it.
I saw Balawi's face and realized this might be the break we've been waiting for—I stood up fast and started moving toward Bradley's office.

I told Jessica I didn't want to be a straphangar—watching the strike from a screen while others were in the field—and when the target disappeared in the feed, I just said, 'Cool. Bring me back a bottle.'
I remember crouching under my desk, the floor cold against my arms, the weight pressing down until I couldn't stay upright anymore.
I told Jack I was going to smoke everyone involved in this op and then kill bin Laden—my voice was steady, but the darkness inside me felt like it had no end.
I slammed my hand on the desk and told them I wanted it to be true—because I did. I needed them to see that this lead was real, even if the evidence wasn't perfect yet.
I was eating my sandwich when Jack called and told me there was no team to deploy—he’s on the phone but nobody’s moving. I said 'Fuck' and just ran.
I stood in the hallway and blocked Bradley’s path because I had to make him see that the caller was our only lead to bin Laden—he had to understand that everything depended on this.
When he told me he didn’t care about bin Laden, I gave him an ultimatum—either send the tech teams to Rawalpindi and Peshawar, or send me back to DC and explain why he killed the operation.

I was sitting at the bar, drinking, feeling like we were stuck—then Jack walked in and put a cloned phone in front of me, saying it would ring every time the target’s phone did. I hugged him and said, 'I love you!'—it was the break we needed.

I stood under the harsh white lights, waiting, listening—then finally heard the sound of the helicopter approaching. When PRINCE 52 came into view and the SEALs emerged with the bag, I knew it was over.
I walked to the body bag alone, unzipped it, and looked at his face—after seven years, it was finally him. I met McRaven’s gaze and nodded; no words were needed.
I sat on the empty plane, buckled in, and when the pilot asked if I was Maya, I just said yes—then couldn’t speak. The weight of it all hit me at once, and I stopped holding it back.
